passage: Sonali had a practical exam in the morning when Saurabh's call lit up her phone at eleven for the third night running. She answered anyway. "I can't sleep, it's all pointless, tell me it's okay." She said the right words in a flat voice, then sat with her notes unread and her jaw tight. She resented him, quietly, and resenting him made her feel like a bad friend. The next afternoon she told the college counsellor everything, resentment included. The counsellor said tiredness like this was human and asked who else was around Saurabh. Sonali rang his older sister and his roommate. Then she told Saurabh gently, "I care about you, but I can't be the only one you call. I'll check in at six every evening." Saurabh was quiet, then said, "Okay."

qa.q: How many nights in a row had Saurabh called at eleven?
qa.a: It was the third night running.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel about herself for resenting Saurabh?
qa.a: Like a bad friend, guilty as well as worn out.

qa.q: What limits did Sonali set, and how do they help?
qa.a: She offered a check-in at six each evening instead of being the only person he calls, and brought in his sister and roommate, so the load is shared.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt hearing that Sonali cannot be the only one he calls?
qa.a: Possibly hurt or afraid of being left, which may be why he went quiet, but she also said she cares and offered a regular check-in.

grounding: The protagonist, exhausted as one friend's only support, resents him and shares the load with others while keeping her limits.

passage:
Counsellor's note, student wellbeing centre.

Ojas came in today, not for himself, he said, but about his roommate Divyansh, who has been low since his parents separated. For two months Ojas has been his only support: late-night talks, food runs, covering attendance. Today Ojas sat with his fists pressed into his knees.

Then, very quietly: "Sometimes I hate him. And I hate myself for that."

I told him that this feeling is common in carers and does not make him a bad friend. It means the load is too heavy for one person.

We made a plan together. Ojas will encourage Divyansh to book his own appointment here; I will make sure a slot is free this week. Ojas will also mention it to Divyansh's elder brother, with Divyansh's knowledge. Ojas will keep two evenings a week for his own football. - Ritu

qa.q: How long has Ojas been Divyansh's only support?
qa.a: Ojas has been his only support for two months.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he pressed his fists into his knees?
qa.a: Ojas felt exhausted and secretly resentful, and also guilty for hating Divyansh sometimes.

qa.q: How does the plan share the load?
qa.a: Divyansh gets his own appointment, his elder brother is brought in, and Ojas keeps two evenings for football, so Ojas is no longer the only support.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel when Ojas suggests he book his own appointment?
qa.a: Divyansh might feel a little pushed away at first, but may also feel cared for, since it gives him more help than one tired friend can.

grounding: The counsellor's note shows a young man worn out and resentful from being a friend's only support, learning to share the load and keep limits.

passage:
Sunday, 11:50 pm

Emil called again at eleven. Third night this week. I'm Noor, and I love Emil like a brother, but tonight while he talked about the breakup for the fortieth time, I muted myself and screamed into a pillow. Then I felt disgusting.

I've cancelled two study groups. I didn't go to my sister's birthday dinner because he texted "I'm not okay." I'm tired in my bones. And angry, which I'm ashamed of.

Elizabeth from our course said something last week: "You can't be his whole support system. That's not fair on either of you."

So tomorrow I'll tell Emil, kindly, that I can talk until ten on weeknights, and that I think he should go to the counselling service. I'll give him the number. I'll also message his brother, like Emil once said I could. Then I'm going to sleep.

qa.q: How many times had Emil called that week, counting tonight?
qa.a: It was the third night that week.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling after screaming into the pillow?
qa.a: Noor felt disgusted and ashamed of the anger, while also being bone-tired from the constant support.

qa.q: What limits does Noor plan, and why are they fair?
qa.a: Noor will talk until ten on weeknights, point Emil to counselling and involve his brother, so Emil gets more help and Noor avoids burning out.

qa.q: How might Emil feel about Noor's new limits?
qa.a: Emil might feel hurt or scared at first, but may later see that more support and a rested friend help him more than one exhausted listener.

grounding: The diary shows a young person resentful after being a friend's only support who plans limits and shares the load with others and professionals.
